name: Umar Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Umar, I'm 27. I'm a junior buyer at Brookline Catering Supply, which sells meat and frozen food to schools, hospitals and canteens. My wife Leila works in a pharmacy, and we've been married two years, no children yet but we'd like them soon. I left school at 18 and worked in my dad's butcher's shop before this, so I know meat better than I know spreadsheets.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in at seven and check the freezer stock against the menus the schools sent. Then I order chicken, mince, fish fingers and so on from about a dozen suppliers, and my boss Gareth signs off big orders. Sometimes I use an AI tool to summarise a long supplier contract, because I'm slow with the small print. I like it when I spot bad meat on a sample and stop an order. The worst bit is the price rows with suppliers, which I'm still learning to win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people got carried away. At work I'd say a buyer still needs to know a good cut from a bad one. I wouldn't post anything; I keep my opinions for the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's what I'd prefer. I use it a bit for contracts and that's enough. I can keep learning the trade properly from Gareth, the way my dad learned from his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep learning, and ask Gareth to let me handle the chicken suppliers on my own. Leila and I would keep saving for a house; we're well past six months of savings already. We'd probably try for a baby next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's how I pictured my life going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong at Brookline even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Food prices, mainly. When feed costs went up last year, chicken jumped and two schools moved to a cheaper supplier. If we keep losing schools, Gareth won't need two buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. A buyer at Brookline still needs to smell the meat and know when a supplier is lying. I'd just get better at it.

I'd say at work that a buyer still needs to **know a good cut**.
think: I'd prefer this; a little AI for **contracts** is enough.
I can keep learning from Gareth, **the way my dad** learned from his.
do: Ask Gareth to let me run the **chicken suppliers** alone.
Keep saving for a **house** and try for a **baby** next year.
feel: **Calm**; it's how he pictured his **life going**.

fieldNote: His real worry is **food prices** and losing school contracts, not AI.

His savings and Leila's job make this world feel **secure**.

steps.text: Ask Gareth to hand over the chicken suppliers

Try for a first baby with Leila next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and you can't stop it, but people should be given a fair chance to adapt. I'd tell the younger lads at the warehouse to learn a trade as well. At church I'd say the same to the families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Buying and checking are on that list, and that's all my desk work. Gareth would keep the experienced buyers, and I'm the junior who still loses the price rows with suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI ordering tools as soon as Brookline brings them in, because if others are using them I'd better too. I'd also go back to my dad's shop on Saturdays to keep my butchery up. Leila and I would hold off on the baby for a year until things are clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be sleeping worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with Leila about the baby go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easy. Leila wants a baby, I want one too. But I want to be sure I've got work before we do. She'd understand, but she wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say come back full time. He's 58 and wants someone to take over the shop. That's my backup, really.

I'd tell younger warehouse lads to also learn **a trade**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and families will suffer. I'd say the government should help businesses keep apprentices, not just hand out money. I'd talk about it at church and with my wife's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my buying job's gone by 2028. If AI can do any thinking work, it can order chicken for a hundred schools. The butcher's shop is hands-on, so it lasts until robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Brookline within months and go full time with my dad, learning to run the shop. We'd use some savings to update the shop, maybe a new counter. Leila and I would put the baby off for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't supermarkets with AI and robots squeeze out a small butcher's too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess so. But people like buying meat from a person who knows them by name. I'd bet on that for a few years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be scared to say to Leila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd failed her. She works hard, she wants a family, and my wife Leila would be waiting on a baby because computers took my job. That would hurt.

I'd say government should help firms keep **apprentices**, not hand out money.
think: The **butcher's shop** is hands-on, so it lasts until robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough, so people should stop talking and start preparing. I'd say young men should learn a trade. I'd say it plainly at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my buying job ends around 2031. But five years means I can take over Dad's shop properly when he retires, instead of in a rush. That's actually not a bad future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brookline two more years, saving hard. I'd work Saturdays at the shop and learn the books and the suppliers. Around 2028 I'd move over full time, and Dad could slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go ahead with a baby in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Leila and I would try for a baby next year. With five years' warning, I can be a dad and a butcher, in that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots come to the shop by 2034, I know. By then I'd have customers who trust me. Maybe I'd add catering for weddings, things that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no need to panic. I'd say families should plan and young people should learn real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be 37, running Dad's shop by then, with children. The robots don't come till 2039, so the shop has years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying at Brookline for four or five years and save. I'd learn the AI tools as they arrive, because they'll help at the shop too. We'd have a baby next year, maybe two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that would still bother you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children. If they're born next year, they'll be 13 when the robots come. I don't know what work there'll be for my son or daughter by the time they're grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to give them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard work, honesty, a trade with their hands. That's what my dad gave me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job goes before I've learned to run the shop, and Leila and I would put our family off. What would help is support for small family businesses to take on apprentices, and lower taxes for shops like Dad's, so they can survive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about my dad. My dad spent forty years building that butcher's shop, and I'd like to keep it going for him, AI or no AI.

headlineQuote: My dad spent forty years building that butcher's shop, and I'd like to keep it going for him, AI or no AI.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** junior buyer at Brookline Catering Supply, married to Leila, a pharmacy worker.
He grew up in his **dad's butcher's shop** and trusts hands-on judgement.
He uses AI now and then and expects his **desk work** to shrink in faster worlds.
His backup is taking over the **family shop**, with timing set by the scenario.
AI timing shapes when he and Leila **have children**, his deepest concern.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job goes before he can run the shop and family plans stall.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **family businesses** to take apprentices, and **lower taxes** for small shops.
